script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Hello, Riverside Fitness Centre. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Hi. I'm interested in a membership. What options do you have?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: We have three types. Standard is for off-peak hours only, that's before four in the afternoon. Premium gives access at any time. And there's a Student option.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Student sounds good. How much is it?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: The student membership is twenty-four pounds a month, and you need to show a valid student card.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Is there a joining fee?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, there's a one-off joining fee of thirty pounds, but it's waived if you pay for twelve months in advance.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Right. Do you have a swimming pool?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: The pool is open from six to ten in the morning and from five until nine in the evening. Lane swimming is in the mornings only.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Can I bring a friend to try it out?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, guests can come once for free if they book in advance by phone.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Great. Can I start on Monday the third?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Certainly. I'll need your full name and date of birth.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Alan Fraser, the fourteenth of March, 1999.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Also, do you offer personal training?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Yes, we have qualified trainers. A one-hour session is priced separately, and you can book one through the app once you've joined. They're popular, so it's worth booking early.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Good to know. Are there lockers in the changing rooms?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: There are lockers in both changing rooms. You'll need a refundable deposit for the key, which you get back when you return it. Towels are provided at the front desk, but there's a small charge for them.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: That's useful. Is there parking?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: There's a car park behind the building, and it's free for members. Bicycles can be locked at the rack near the entrance.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Brilliant. I think I'm sold. Can I sign up today?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: Of course. Let's get the forms completed, and I'll take your photo for the card.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: How long does it take to get the card?

script.speaker: Receptionist
script.text: The card is printed while you wait, so you can use it straight away.

title: Guided Tour of the Botanic Garden

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Welcome to the Eastbank Botanic Garden. I'll outline the tour and a few rules before we begin.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The tour lasts about seventy minutes and covers four zones. We begin in the tropical glasshouse, which is kept at twenty-six degrees.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: After that, we walk to the herb garden, then the rose walk, and finish in the old orchard. The orchard is closed to visitors in winter, so the tour doesn't go there from December to February.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Please don't touch the plants. The only exception is the scented herb garden, where you may rub the leaves gently.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Cameras are welcome, but flash photography is not allowed inside the glasshouse because it can harm the orchids.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Refreshments are available at the café near the gate. The café closes at four, half an hour before the garden does.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The garden itself closes at half past four. If you lose anything, please come to the information desk by the main gate.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Next month we'll run a special night tour, but that requires a separate ticket costing fifteen pounds.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The glasshouse also houses a collection of carnivorous plants. Some of them catch insects, and you may see them digesting prey if you look closely near the back wall.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The rose walk is at its best in early summer. The roses are labelled with their names and the year they were introduced, so take a moment to read the boards.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Benches are placed along the walk, and you're welcome to sit and rest. Please keep to the paths, because the beds are fragile and easily damaged.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Children are welcome, but they should be supervised at all times, especially near the pond, which is quite deep.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: There's a shop at the exit selling seeds, plant guides and small gifts. Card payments are accepted, but cash is not.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Thank you for coming today. I hope you enjoy the garden, and please give us your feedback on the way out.

title: Planning a River Water Quality Project

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Sam, have you settled on your group's research question for the environmental science project?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: We think we'll look at river water quality near the town, specifically nitrate levels.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. Where are you taking samples?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Three sites: upstream of the factory, below the factory, and at the weir. We'll take samples every Tuesday for four weeks.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Why Tuesdays in particular?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: The river authority publishes flow data on Tuesdays, and we want to match our samples to the flow.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's sensible. For the field tests, what method are you using?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: We're using test strips in the field and sending a few samples to the lab to check them.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Test strips are less accurate, so your report must mention that as a limitation.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: We know. That's why we'll compare them with the lab results.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: How many samples in total?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Twelve per site, so thirty-six altogether, plus three blanks.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: And who is doing the statistics?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Dan will do the statistics. I'll write the methods section and the limitations.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: When is the draft due?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: The draft is due on the twentieth of November, and we're presenting on the fourth of December.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Have you thought about the risks in the field, such as weather or access to the weir?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Yes. We'll wear waders for the weir, and we'll never sample alone. We've also added a backup day in case of heavy rain.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Good. Make sure the risk assessment is signed before the first visit.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: We already have the form. Dan is collecting signatures from the lab technician this week.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: Excellent. And what will you do if a result looks odd?

script.speaker: Student
script.text: We'll repeat the test on a fresh sample and record both results, so the report shows that we checked.

script.speaker: Tutor
script.text: That's the right approach. Keep your field notebook up to date as well; examiners look at it.

script.speaker: Student
script.text: Will do. Thanks for the feedback.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today we'll look at pollinator decline, specifically honeybees and wild bees.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Pollination supports about one third of the food crops that people eat, according to most estimates.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: This matters for both farmers and consumers, because crops such as apples, berries and many oilseeds produce better yields when they are visited by a good variety of insects.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Researchers identify three main pressures on pollinators: habitat loss, pesticides, and disease.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Habitat loss is the most significant of the three. As farmland spreads, hedgerows and wildflower meadows disappear, and bees lose nesting sites and food.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Pesticides are a second factor. Some neonicotinoid chemicals are harmful even at low doses, although regulations now restrict their use in several regions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The third pressure is disease, particularly the Varroa mite, which weakens honeybee colonies by spreading viruses.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Climate change is also emerging as a factor. Flowering times are shifting, so some bees arrive when no flowers are available.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Warmer winters can also confuse insects that normally stay dormant until spring, so the timing problem works in both directions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Some people assume that honeybees are the most important pollinators. In fact, many wild species, including solitary bees, are often more efficient pollinators for particular crops.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Solutions include planting wildflower strips along field edges, reducing pesticide use during flowering periods, and creating nest sites such as bare soil banks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Several of these measures cost little. A farmer can leave a corner of a field uncut, and a council can change the way it mows roadside verges, without any large investment.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let me say a little more about wild bees. There are thousands of species, and most of them are solitary. They do not produce honey or live in large colonies, which means they are often overlooked by the public.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Different bees pollinate different plants. Some species visit only a few types of flower, while others feed on a wide range. This specialisation can make some bees vulnerable when their preferred plants disappear.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Research methods have also changed. Scientists now use photographs taken by volunteers, along with DNA analysis of pollen collected from bees' bodies, to work out which plants each species depends on.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: This kind of work was once very slow, because each specimen had to be identified by an expert under a microscope. Digital tools have made it possible to process far more records than a small team could manage alone.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Public engagement is an important part of the work. Many local groups run survey days, where families can learn to identify bees and record what they see in gardens and parks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Gardeners can help too. Leaving some areas of lawn to grow long, planting a range of flowers across the seasons, and avoiding unnecessary chemicals all make a difference.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Finally, remember that these measures are complementary. No single action will solve the problem, so policy, farming practice and individual behaviour all need to work together.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Next session we'll compare these approaches with the policies used in three European countries, and you should read the assigned case studies before then. Please also bring your questions about the survey design, because we'll discuss them at the start of the session. The reading list is available on the course page.
